section.title: Ethan Evans: Corporate Politics, Reorgs, Promotions, and Leverage at Amazon
section.deck: Former Amazon VP Ethan Evans explains how empire building, reorgs, scope fights, firings and promotions actually work, and how to use influence, timing and careful wording to get what you need.

blocks.text: Ethan Evans, a former Amazon vice president, returns for a second conversation with Ryan and argues that corporate politics is a learnable skill set rather than an optional extra. In Ethan's account, reorgs, promotions, scope fights and firings are shaped by incentives, stories and relationships as much as by technical merit. His advice is to read other people's motives, prepare careful wording before a hard conversation, build leverage so that a request is hard to refuse, and treat the person across the table as a human being rather than an obstacle. The examples are Ethan's own experience at Amazon and with coaching clients. Figures, legal points and claims about other companies are his recollection or second-hand reports, not verified facts.
blocks.heading: Politics as a skill: motives, narratives, leverage and relationships (Ethan's view)

blocks.question: What is empire building, and why does it persist at large companies?
answer: Ethan defines empire building as focusing on raw headcount rather than on what a team does or the impact it has. He says it exists because it is rewarded, and it is rewarded because counting people is the easiest thing to do. Impact is subjective: one leader may think a project was hard and another may think it was easy. Nobody can argue with the fact that one manager has 42 people and another has 17.

Ethan adds that some companies write headcount thresholds into the criteria for promotion. High performers given such a target will find a way to hit it, including by claiming they need people or by taking over other groups, and they will rationalize that to themselves.

followups.question: Can managers be promoted on impact rather than on how many recursive reports they have?
answer: Ethan says it is possible but takes more effort, because a manager's impact is fuzzy. A leader must decide what counts most: operational performance, features shipped, or whether those features make money. He gives the example of one product that directly earns revenue and another that is infrastructure keeping systems up. Comparing the two is hard.

Value judgments are also harder to defend than headcount. Telling someone that a peer was more impactful tends to make them angry unless they happen to agree. Ethan says that is why impact assessment is dangerous and gets done less than it should.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Do written headcount thresholds exist for senior manager, director and VP at Amazon?
answer: Ethan says no thresholds were written down while he was there. They existed as whispered numbers. After he left, people he coached at Amazon told him that the director number had become 90 in some organizations. Ethan became a director in the early days with 22 people. By the end of his career he sensed that the company wanted about 75 or 80.

Ethan points to an irony: one Amazon leadership principle says there is no bonus for additional headcount, yet once a number is written down, reaching it carries a pay reward that he describes as several hundred thousand dollars a year. He has heard of bosses placing people under a leader for six months to cross the threshold, then returning them. Ethan calls that insanity.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: After the promotion, must the leader keep those reports?
answer: Not strictly, Ethan says. At Amazon there is a grace period of six to nine months if a leader can tell a story about how the team will regrow. He knows of no company that systematically down-levels people. Instead, a leader whose team is no longer director scope is told to find a director-level role, which the boss can arrange in the same organization or by moving the person. Ethan has seen headcount shuffled this way at Amazon and elsewhere.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Do reorgs often carry a second, unstated motive, such as getting someone promoted?
answer: Ethan says there is always something else going on. Leaders know that too many reorgs cost them people, so they wait as long as they can. When they finally act, they ask how to get everything they want: how to give less to someone they would like to see move on, set up a high performer, and keep key people. Once the business case is settled, he says, the question becomes what else can be loaded onto the ship before it leaves the dock. He notes that people often come to him saying a boss told them they were being placed under a peer so that the peer would have enough scope for promotion.

Because a reorg is usually large enough that someone will audit it, Ethan says the leader must build a narrative: the reorg rewards the deserving, meets the business goals, and any pain lands on people who are not top performers. He recalls his own reorgs as mostly about retention, asking who he must keep and who he could live with losing. He cannot recall putting someone in a role expecting them to quit, but he can recall using a reorg to give a person at risk of leaving something more attractive.

followups.question: What usually triggers a reorg?
answer: Ethan names two main triggers. The first is a change in the business, such as a new market, an acquired company to blend in, or a new project. The second is a cascade: someone else quit or was moved. Several times in his career his own boss left, and he could go up if judged ready, move under someone different, or the role could be backfilled. At Amazon he says he never saw a backfill happen; he was always moved under another leader.

When his leader left while Ethan ran the Prime Video team, he was moved from an engineering VP to a business leader. That leader said early on that he did not want to run engineering. Ethan feared the worst, but says the leader became one of his best managers and they had a great run. He adds that being the guinea pig for a non-technical leader can be demoralizing, and he is fairly sure he was sometimes placed under people in order to stretch them.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Is the hidden chess of selling different parts of a reorg to different people avoidable for managers?
answer: Ethan says a manager can work around it by reorganizing purely on business goals and ignoring people. He expects that to cost the manager people, because some employees are more ambitious or demanding than others. The leader is aware of what each stakeholder wants to hear and which parts of the plan can be sold to whom.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Does the squeaky wheel get the grease in reorgs and promotions?
answer: Ethan says there is truth in the old saying, and that people do not like this harsh fact. If two people perform about equally and one has made clear they are thinking of leaving, a manager may reason that the loyal one will wait another six months. That manager then uses those six months to save the other person. It is not meant to hurt the quiet employee, Ethan says, but that person can fall behind simply for being nice.

He often tells coaching clients that they are very nice and that, in this context, it is not a compliment. Ethan does not say people need to be jerks. Pushy people get more up to a point, and beyond it they antagonize and get less. In a reorg, he adds, a leader may serve the pushy people first because that keeps the whole team intact, while assuming the quiet people will be fine.

followups.question: How should a leader respond to a manager who is clearly empire building to reach promotion?
answer: Ethan says the leader should first have a trusting relationship, then talk privately and honestly. He would say that he understands the manager is empire building and trying to reach a goal, but that this particular request goes too far. Then he tries to turn the discussion into problem solving: how can they reach the goal by a defensible path?
Ethan prefers this to a flat no, which would frustrate the manager and start an argument. He admits he is not always successful, since some people want what they want right now and have no patience.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: How did Ethan tell his own manager that he expected to be promoted?
answer: Ethan was a senior manager with 22 people and wanted to become a director at Amazon. He told his manager, Neil, that his career was very important to him and that he needed to understand how important it was to Amazon, because if it was less important to Amazon than to him, he would need to think about that. Ethan says nobody can argue with a statement that his career matters to him, and the last line signals he has options without being a direct threat. He was promoted.

Ethan's general point is that there is a middle ground that makes clear what you want and that you will consider other options, without being a threatening jerk. He adds that the right message depends on the workplace. Amazon was sharp-elbowed, so this line was not offensive there, while it would be in some other places. Part of the answer, he says, is finding a place where you look like a sweet person in the mix.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Did demanding high performers ever irritate Ethan so much that he refused them?
answer: Ethan gives two answers. First, if a very demanding person has become a net negative, a flat no will usually make them quit, even for a lesser job, because they are driven to get what they want. There is a calculation about which answer produces the result the leader needs.

Second, Ethan preferred to make a deal. He would tell a high performer that he would help them get what they wanted if they delivered exceptional results on what he needed. He says he always followed through, with one early-career exception that he still regrets after about twenty years.

followups.question: Can you give an example of a deal you made?
answer: Ethan's vice president told him, as a director, that his team was too expensive and he should open a low-cost offshore development center. The boss did not name a country, so the whole problem fell to Ethan, who did not want to travel the world setting up teams.

Ethan approached a senior manager he knew who wanted to become a director and was an Indian living in the United States. He asked whether that manager would move to India to start a center, and said the center could become the platform for a promotion to director. The manager moved for three years, and Ethan then used his independent work to write a story showing director-level accomplishment, and he was promoted. Ethan stresses that the deal was made years before it paid off.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: What if circumstances change and you can no longer deliver on such a deal?
answer: Ethan says that if he had been reorganized or fired, he would have told the person that he no longer had the power to deliver, though he would support them as far as he could. He cannot recall a case where he failed this way. He thinks most leaders are professionals who can tell the difference between not coming through and being unable to.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Do managers keep a queue of who is up for promotion next?
answer: Ethan says there is a line, and big companies often have a policy on it. At Amazon, HR tracked a forward-looking slate of promotions by half-year, with names projected at six, twelve, eighteen and sometimes twenty-four months. There was a sense of whose turn it was, though he says there was no strict quota in his time.

He says someone he coached at Google described a strict quota, for example two people moving from L8 to L9 in an organization in a given half. Ethan notes that this is a second-hand report. In his view, quotas appear mainly at rare, expensive senior levels, where a position such as staff, principal or distinguished engineer can cost around a million dollars a year. Early-career levels usually have no quota.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: How should a leader handle someone in the organization who tries to take scope from a colleague?
answer: Ethan says this has become more common as growth has slowed. When a company is growing quickly, as Amazon did for much of his tenure, it is easier to get new people than to fight over existing ones. In flat-headcount companies, he describes more cannibalism. His answer is that a leader cannot let a team member act as a pirate who captures another person's ship, because that leaves the leader looking clueless and no longer in charge. The leader has to find the person a path, convince them to wait, or, if they turn toxic, let them become the one who leaves.

Ethan notes that blatant self-service is restrained by the risk of getting caught. His advice to people who want more is to tell their manager in advance that they are interested and ready to step up if an opening appears, and that they intend to stay. Reorgs shake things up, and managers worry about placing someone in a role who then leaves. Ethan says a person who signals they will stay becomes the most reliable candidate, not necessarily the best.

followups.question: Is that a better way to ask for scope than saying give me that team?
answer: Ethan agrees. He says there is a polite fiction that can also be true: the person wants what is best for the organization and understands that the best path up is to be valuable to the leader. Telling a manager that whatever the reorg brings, the person will be there for them sounds selfless, even though the underlying message may be that the person wants more scope and will take whatever is available. One sounds like a pirate ship and the other like a servant, but both mean the same thing.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Doesn't that feel conniving?
answer: Ethan says it can be conniving, but it does not have to be. Someone can honestly tell a manager that they want to grow and will do whatever is needed to grow, and that can be both honest and strategic.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Did you take on scope that way yourself?
answer: Ethan describes working toward VP under a leader who had no other engineering managers and kept being handed engineering work. Ethan built trust with that boss and was given everything, ending up with about eight different functions and 200 people. They included technical work for the reverse logistics of used video games, game downloads, the start of Amazon's Appstore, and a business-to-business effort to sell office supplies in bulk. Ethan says he did not particularly want to grade video games or ship pallets of paper, but saying yes to everything was a win-win. Ryan notes the similarity to the offshore story: the boss had work he did not want and passed it to a high performer.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: What is the simplest rule for getting promoted?
answer: Ethan repeats advice from a former Amazon senior vice president, now at Walmart, that the simple way to get promoted is to solve problems for your boss. A boss who values you does not want to lose you, and most people are just punching the clock. Ethan says that even a self-interested boss will want to keep the people who help them.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: What about engineers who create scope by finding a problem nobody asked them to solve?
answer: Ethan says that can also work, and that he recommends both paths: ask your manager how you can help, and also think about what you could do on your own. His example is custom-printed t-shirts, which he says Amazon now sells at over a billion dollars a year. Ethan helped start the business and funded the first team out of his Appstore organization. His boss asked what t-shirt printing had to do with the Appstore.

Ethan told his boss that he saw a big business there and needed 10 people out of 800. If he could not spend about one percent of his resources on something he believed in, Ethan said, that would be micromanagement. The boss disagreed but agreed. Ethan says about 790 of his 800 people worked on what his manager wanted and 10 on his own bet, and that a leader who runs side projects must shut failures quickly and keep a good hit rate. His summary is that there are multiple paths to the top, and he tried them all: be the helpful person, and also be the inventor.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: How are reorgs used to manage certain leaders out?
answer: Ethan says in practice a leader puts the person on something they do not want to work on and claims it was the only seat available. He tells of an early Amazon group where leaders owned Prime Video, Prime Music, the Kindle and an ingestion pipeline. One leader was given database maintenance, quality assurance and a few small items, and joked that his group was Other. The VP objected to calling it the garbage can, but Ethan believes the VP expected that leader to leave. The leader, calm and a team player, was reportedly still at Amazon twenty years later.

Ethan's view is that giving a pushy, overly ambitious person the Other seat can create a vacancy within weeks. He himself tended to fire people directly, but he calls the bad-seat move classic and not unique to Amazon. In Japanese culture, as Ethan understands it (he says he is not an expert), a window seat signals exile from the center of action, the opposite of how Americans see a corner office.

followups.question: Can a vice president build an organization that rewards the nice people who wait their turn?
answer: Ethan says to some degree, but he points out that the broad organization he described was itself a garbage can he opted into, taking all the leftover work. He sees two problems with rewarding only nice people. Some nice people do not want more, and ambitious people tend to become more vocal. Vocal people also will not simply become quiet because he rewards niceness; they will look for somewhere that rewards them right away. He says a better leader might build that culture, but he does not think it fits human nature.

His usual response is to tell nice clients that being that nice is not helping them. They do not need to be a jerk. They can say that their career is very important to them. He observes this is hard for people from collectivist, non-US cultures, citing women from parts of Asia expected to prioritize family at home and then to speak up at work. His message is that it is acceptable to ask for what you want, and that even good managers are not in the business of guessing. The person who knocks on the door every three days is the one whose wishes are clear.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: What should an engineer do about a weak manager: can they go to the manager's boss?
answer: Ethan says escalations like this reach him all the time, and that employees underestimate how the skip-level boss thinks. A boss hearing about a weakness in a direct report faces two options. One is to decide the complainer is overly sensitive and high maintenance, in which case the problem is the complainer, and the boss can pass it back to the manager. The other is to agree, which creates three problems: deciding what to do with the manager, hiring and training a replacement, and doing the manager's work in the meantime. Even if it is subconscious, he says, the boss has many reasons not to believe easily.

So his advice is never to mutiny alone. If the employee really wants action, they should bring two or three colleagues, or send them in sequence. He describes a leader who treated the women on the team badly. A lone report would probably have been ignored, but when Ethan asked several women and they confirmed it, he realized he had been blind to a problem and acted.

followups.question: Should the engineer build allies first rather than going straight to the skip?
answer: Yes, Ethan says. Talking to colleagues first is a sanity check: if they get along fine with the manager, the engineer may learn something about adjusting to style. If they share the experience, the next hurdle is whether they are willing to speak up, and many people are not. Ethan suggests the engineer offer to go first as ringleader and tell the skip that three named colleagues can verify the story. Most managers, though not all, will agree to talk to them.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: What if the engineer just says the move would be more productive for the organization and avoids criticizing the manager?
answer: Ethan offers two approaches. First, if the engineer can make a plausible case that they would be as valuable or more valuable elsewhere, they need not mention the manager at all. Second, think several moves ahead and keep it blame-free: say that the fit with the current leader is not working, that the fault may be either side, and that a change is needed.

He used this once at Amazon. His boss wanted him to stay in a role he was doing well, while Ethan wanted a new role in the same organization. He explained that the real choice was not between staying and moving but between moving within this boss's organization and moving elsewhere. After weeks of resistance, he was in the new role the next morning.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: How did you word that without making the boss feel forced?
answer: Ethan says he framed it in terms of what the boss would do. He had a job offer from a senior vice president in another organization, and he told his own VP that once he gave his word to that executive he would have to go, because the boss would do the same in his position. Ethan said he wanted the other role, had been told no several times, and asked what the boss wanted him to do. The boss understood he would never break his word to an SVP, so he understood that the choice was keep Ethan or lose him. Ethan did not say it as a threat. He says he was careful to say only that once he gave his word, he could not go back.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: How can someone find careful wording for these conversations, such as the polite fictions Ethan has described?
answer: Ethan says he is not sure how to teach this, but one common mistake is not thinking through wording before entering the room. Most of these conversations are not spur of the moment: they are on the calendar, like a performance review, or are known to be coming. He advises preparing a key phrase in advance so that it can be said with sincerity. In his examples nothing was a lie, yet he delivered the lines warmly. He says delivery matters as much as content: the same words with a hard tone provoke a hostile reaction, and the same words with a warm one do not.
To engineers who say they hate politics, Ethan replies that this is simply human interaction, with other people's emotions, defensiveness and stress, and that they should get good at it.

followups.question: Can that skill be reverse engineered?
answer: Ethan says it applies to any negotiation or deal. He calls his approach being interpersonally warm while professionally firm: friendly, smiling and not agitated, but clear about what he really wants, without anger or a you-versus-me tone. One key phrase is to ask for help, because people enjoy seeing themselves as helpful, and asking how someone can help is different from asking what they will do for you.

He says the attitude comes from Leadership and Self-Deception, from the Arbinger Institute. Its lesson, as Ethan reads it, is to see the other person as a human trying to do their best rather than as an obstacle. He can then say what he needs, ask what the other person needs, and offer to help.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: How does that apply when you need another team to do something?
answer: Ethan says engineers often objectify other teams by treating them like an API: make the right call and get the right result. He suggests instead acknowledging the other team's busy roadmap and asking how to help them make time or how to make the change themselves. Once people feel cared about, they usually respond in kind.

He adds that nothing works every time. In a recent debate with a college roommate over contentious politics, his best techniques failed to persuade, though both left friendly. Sometimes the other person's motives cannot align with yours.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Is there a simple rule set, or does it come down to judgment?
answer: Ryan suggests the unifying idea is imagining what the other person feels. Ethan offers a chess analogy, noting he is not an expert. A good player knows the board and also has memorized opening moves. In a conversation, he says, a person can prepare opening moves: how to make the first ask and when. He would not raise a career discussion minutes after a severe problem on a Friday when a manager is rushing out. After the opening, general principles apply, such as moving toward common ground, as a chess player moves toward the center.

He adds that early in his career he had a temper and was fired twice and put on a layoff list for being volatile and critical. Putting the temper away made a large difference, he says, because people respond poorly to anger or criticism even when the speaker is right.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.label: Ethan's working formula (editorial summary)
blocks.text: Ethan describes his approach as being interpersonally warm and professionally firm: friendly, calm delivery; honest statements of what he wants; no anger or us-versus-them framing; asking how the other person can help; treating the other person as a human rather than a lever; and preparing phrases and timing in advance.

blocks.question: When a manager or colleague is a skilled influencer, is that a positive sign or a warning?
answer: Both, Ethan says. He argues that the skills of influence and politics are the same, and that the difference is motive. He teaches executive presence and points out that Darth Vader had plenty of it. When he meets a skilled operator, he asks which side they are on. There are three cases: people with good motives, who are easy to work with; people entirely out for themselves, whom he compares to the Sith; and a middle group whose motives are workable. With the third group he can make deals: they are not altruistic, but they want something he can help with, and the two can ship something or earn something together without being friends.

followups.question: Would you still ally with an extreme high performer who would drop you the moment it helped them?
answer: Ethan says he would separate if he could, but at work people often cannot choose which teams they need. Sometimes a team is run by a terrible or self-serving person. He advises minimizing contact where possible but also learning to work even with very unethical people, short of breaking laws.

Among the protections he lists is bringing allies. Slippery people prefer to operate in the dark and usually cannot afford for everyone to know they are unethical, since they would be shunned. So he suggests constructing a situation where it is easier for them to go along than to fight, such as one with many witnesses. He is sorry this frustrates engineers but says humans have always been mean to each other and engineers will have to deal with it.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: So the best protection against backstabbing is soft power that makes you too costly to attack?
answer: Ethan agrees and compares it to a porcupine: many animals could eat one, but the mouthful of quills is not worth it. He adds that slippery people do not wake up thinking they are evil jerks. Their self-narrative is that they are practical and others are wishy-washy. He suggests helping them with that narrative, telling them that the practical move is to help you because you are a rising star who will remember it. He says the main point is that people he calls unethical tell themselves a story in which they are not villains, so understanding that story offers a way to redirect them.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Have other organizations tried to take scope from Ethan's organization, and how can a leader defend against that?
answer: Ethan says he saw it all the time. In his account the people trying to take scope rarely think of themselves as pillagers. They know their own mission well, so they see clearly how your scope would help them, while not understanding your mission, so they can imagine that your organization is not important. He quotes a smart engineering leader who said respect between two engineering teams is inversely proportional to their distance. He gives the example of Amazon S3, which stores hundreds of trillions of objects and is sometimes dismissed as a big disk drive; the closer you get, the more complexity you see. Few people plan to be evil, he says; they want something and construct a line of logic for why it is good.

He lists defensive tactics. The skunk trick is to make yourself unattractive: list the unglamorous things you maintain that the other team does not know about, and have customers explain how important they are. Another is to be thorny, so that the attacker looks for a softer target, though he warns that behaving in a way that discredits you makes you an easier target. A third is to expose motives while making a strong case for the value of your work, which is easier from a base of strong performance. A fourth is delay: reorgs cost about six months of productivity, so a team that is hitting its goals can argue that now is the wrong time. Ethan says the common thread is narrative, because people reach an emotional conclusion and then rationalize it, so the better storyteller wins.

followups.question: What are the attacker tactics if a strong manager thinks another organization should be absorbed?
answer: Ethan jokes that Ryan was not kidding about transparency. He says the best attack is a real story of how the merger will create more value, for example doubling a release rate or doubling revenue and how. Slightly weaker arguments are about seniority, efficiency, cost savings, simplicity or fewer direct reports for the decision maker. Ethan says these second-order arguments are not false but make things smoother for the leader rather than growing the business.

The third tactic, which he hopes nobody uses but knows people do, is to highlight flaws in the other organization. If the problems are true, he prefers to approach the owner or common boss and ask if there is anything he can do to help. He calls that his opening gambit for taking over. After he helps and things improve, he can casually mention that, now that he sees the efficiencies, they could consolidate.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: What can a leader do about a well-liked person in another organization who is a major problem for their own organization?
answer: Ethan says one of his managers once assigned a person he called a meat shield, whose job was to keep that difficult person away from the rest of the group until a project finished. The manager was honest that it was a terrible role and promised to make it up later. Ethan says that if you want to change things, the most important step is to understand why the person is valued in their own organization. Their leaders are probably thinking the person has sharp elbows but gets a lot done, and that others are soft.

He then describes two discussions. One is to say we want the value without the pain and ask for a better way. The other is to say the person is mistreating the team and either the interface changes or cooperation will stop. Ethan's private version is to retaliate with delays and process. His outward version is polite: the colleague is valued, but the team is struggling, and Ethan offers a new point of contact or, otherwise, distance between the teams, which will create friction that takes both leaders' time. He notes he has people ready to leave and asks what the other leader would do in his place. Ethan says this is the same message with no threat, and that leaders at that level sense the unspoken stick without needing to hear it. He compares this to telling a rough opponent in ice hockey that he also has elbows.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Why does an engineer need a manager who can stand up for the organization, and what can the engineer do if the manager will not?
answer: Ethan says a manager does not need to be mean to be firm, but does need to be skilled. Many people can only deliver hard messages after working themselves into anger. He tries to stick to his beliefs without using anger as fuel, while admitting that friends tell him when he has been a jerk. He repeats an image that managers are either an umbrella or a funnel, and a funnel passes pressure to the team. A yes-man manager chooses between pushing back on their boss, which feels dangerous, and pushing on the engineer, who has less rank.

Ethan says the engineer has to change the balance of safety: either help the manager feel safe pushing back on their boss, or make it feel unsafe to ask for a fourth weekend. Ryan thinks the first option sounds almost impossible. Ethan replies that the second option is exactly how a manager gets a backbone. He gives a sample script for weekend work: raise the pattern, offer data, say that family is important and that the engineer cannot keep working weekends, and ask how to plan the pushback next time so the manager is not left having committed to work that will not happen.

followups.question: Does that message feel threatening, and when should you raise it?
answer: Ethan agrees that it was not as polished as his other lines and says he could improve it in five minutes. His main correction is timing. The wrong time is while the request is in hand. A better time is Tuesday or Wednesday, after the weekend and before the next crisis. The engineer must also make clear the limit of their tolerance, and that only works if the engineer can accept hearing quit if you don't like it. Ethan says that when he approached his manager about his career he was also looking for outside jobs and was prepared to leave.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: What if the engineer is easy to discard and has little leverage?
answer: Ethan says leverage is required, but good engineers are valuable, and teams that burn through people are not effective. If a company's attitude is bring them in, burn them out and move them on, he says the person is probably in the wrong place. He argues people get trapped believing no better option exists, though he does not belittle hard job searches or the difficulty of entry-level roles in an AI era.

His advice is not to be a victim. He names Extreme Ownership by Jocko Willink as one framing. A person can weather a bad manager while finishing a training program or searching for another job, and Ethan believes that to work less later, people often have to work more first. He closes with an image: a lever that is long enough needs little force, so a person with strong leverage can be polite and soft in their hints.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: What is backchanneling, and when does it help?
answer: Ethan separates good backchanneling from manipulative backchanneling. Manipulative backchanneling is doing something you would not say in public, such as undermining a proposal or painting another leader negatively. He says that is usually unnecessary and he would like to say never necessary. Positive backchanneling is giving people a chance to ask questions and share concerns without having to do so publicly. A finance person worried about the budget, for example, can ask in private rather than in a meeting.

Ethan says it works not only because information is exchanged but because the other person feels understood, consulted and heard, and that emotional buy-in builds trust. When an executive chooses between two similar proposals, he explains, the executive asks who they can count on, how the decision will make them look, and how conflicts will be resolved. A leader who consulted them can win even if the other proposal pays slightly more. Ethan contrasts this with backroom deals, such as kickbacks, which he describes as a proposal to do something wrong because both parties benefit. He says some people accept because they tell themselves they are owed, and that if you can learn their story, you have a better chance to redirect it.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Can influence come from somewhere other than the number of recursive reports?
answer: Ethan says he has seen soft power come from ideas. Amazon built a storage product called Cloud Drive, which he compares to Dropbox or Box, and the proposal came from a newly graduated engineer. The engineer won an invite to an engineering conference, emailed Jeff Bezos to ask him to visit the poster, and pitched the idea. Bezos liked it and emailed the engineer's triple-skip manager, a VP who was Ethan's own boss. That VP disliked the idea, but Bezos had said to look into it, so Ethan funded the project and it got built. Ethan also mentions a slightly more senior colleague who helped put forward the Amazon Fire TV proposal after doing legwork and building connections.

Ethan says the common thread is a story: a vision told as an understandable soundbite that nobody disagrees with, such as having a cloud storage system or a low-cost living room device. It usually starts with real facts, is told with enthusiasm and repeated, and is told to people who have the power to act.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: What are the least discussed reasons that people get fired, beyond what appears in performance notes?
answer: Ethan says there are legal rules about when and how a person can be fired, so the public story is almost always about performance. He says the unspoken reason is often incompatibility of style: detail-oriented versus high-level, or technology-first versus business-outcome-first. A small difference can become a debate that turns into labels, such as technically clueless or only about money. Once a person is labeled, he says, everything they do is read through that lens, and that is where people get fired, though it is always called performance.

He also describes a case in which a newly hired executive at a very senior level was reported by several women, including an HR representative, for sexual harassment, and was terminated right away. Ethan explains why such people can be hired again elsewhere: the company had no legal proof, so naming the person risks a lawsuit, and a former employer typically confirms only dates of employment. Ethan says he later saw that the executive left the Amazon job off a resume, and he does not believe it was a one-off.

followups.question: Can a skip-level boss overrule a manager who wants to fire someone?
answer: Ethan says he has seen a manager float the idea and a skip-level offer to move the person elsewhere. He would say that he knows the employee does well in other environments and could move them out of the manager's hair, without saying the employee would be great elsewhere, which would hint the manager was at fault. He says this makes it socially easy to agree and is as good as firing from his viewpoint.

Ethan adds that it relies on the skip understanding that the problem may be incompatibility, with a manager and report like cats and dogs in a bag. That does not necessarily mean the manager is bad; it means they lack adaptability. He says some people loved managers who drove him crazy, and style does matter.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Do organizations feel like they are held together by duct tape and well-worded phrases?
answer: Ethan smiles and says he feels that way. He compares it to an architecture diagram: when a project starts, the boxes are neat, and when it ships, there are special cases and forgotten items. Managers likewise start out wanting to manage only by performance and develop everyone, then reality arrives with schedules, difficult people, locations and leave, and they are happy if it mostly works. He cites the military phrase that the enemy gets a vote and Mike Tyson's line that everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: Why is it harder to fire a bad manager than a bad engineer, and how does Ethan do it?
answer: Ethan says he agrees it is harder, for three reasons. First, managers tend to be more experienced, so their weaknesses are subtle. The first person he ever fired had stopped coming to work, which was easy. Second, a manager's work is hard to measure: hiring, reviews, shipped features or bug counts all have limits, so the conversation becomes a he-said, she-said problem. Third, managers understand the system and can quickly position themselves to be hard to remove. Ethan still terminated a large number of managers.

His ideal method, which he could not always use, was to raise socially that things may not be working and ask whether the manager would like help finding a better place. Smart managers hear that their boss is unhappy and is offering a door, perhaps with time to find a job or a severance package. He avoided the words fired or performance because, as he understands it, they can create a legal issue called constructive termination. A smooth manager will answer that they are sorry the boss is dissatisfied and are open to changes, which Ethan reads as the start of a counter-negotiation. The other route is formal performance management, with documented expectations and misses. He says almost all managers quit before that finishes, since the process gives them roughly 90 days to find a job.

followups.question: What leverage does someone have when they are being fired, and why would a company pay severance?
answer: Ethan says there are several pieces. First, the formal process costs the manager a lot of time: documentation, paperwork and HR audits, and the employee can string things out. The first offer is to save the manager that time in exchange for money to search for another job. The second is the story the departing person will tell: a terrible experience, or a graceful move on that credits the manager. Ethan phrases it as asking which story the manager wants told to coworkers.

A third piece, he says, is that managers want to feel good about themselves. They can spend a little company money and tell themselves that although it didn't work out, they took care of the person. Ethan also advises buying time: if a hard performance conversation begins when you are not in a good frame of mind, ask for it the next morning. Most managers agree, and if one refuses, HR may sympathize with the employee. He adds that you may get nothing, but if you do not ask, you certainly will not.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Can someone recover from a performance improvement plan?
answer: Ethan says clients write to him after being placed on a plan and ask how to survive. He tells them honestly that they will most likely be fired. By the time a formal plan is given, he says, the manager has tried everything else and wants the person gone quietly. He says managers hate firing and delay, and when they finally act they have told themselves they are out of options. People often write back months later to say he was right, though he acknowledges exceptions.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Can most people deliver the severance message to a manager who already has a negative view of them?
answer: Ryan doubts they can, especially for the team-health version, which is more of a threat. Ethan agrees that people skills matter more than engineers want to believe. He says IQ without emotional intelligence is a waste, and notes the irony that Cal Newport, author of So Good They Can't Ignore You, has the social skills to teach at Princeton and write books. Ethan offers a gentler script: the message is hard, he has many friends on the team, he does not want them to think it is an unfair place, and he asks for help with a graceful exit. He says hard messages need not be delivered cold, because time can be bought to prepare a few phrases.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: How can someone break out of the staff-engineer or front-line manager level where many people get stuck?
answer: Ethan says this is his bread and butter. People get stuck because they keep doing the current skill harder rather than learning the skill of the next level. What gets someone promoted early is hard, effective delivery. Later they need to delegate, communicate and let go of hard skills, because micromanaging drives away good engineers. He points to Marshall Goldsmith's What Got You Here Won't Get You There.

His practical advice is to talk to people a level or two above and ask what they had to let go of and learn, and what they see holding the person back. He prefers asking for advice to asking for feedback, since feedback asks people to criticize and advice invites a more positive version of the same information. He sees many people working brutally hard but ineffectively.

followups.question: If two equally qualified people on the same team want one promotion slot, how can one position first?
answer: Ethan says the differences are relationship and trust. A senior leader has no time to micromanage and needs to hand work over and assume it will be handled well, not necessarily done the way they would do it. Trust, he says, is earned more in bad times than in good, like soldiers who fought together. At work the equivalent is a crisis such as an outage, a lost account or a big embarrassment, where someone shows dedication at a cost to themselves. The leader remembers who came through.

The second factor is whether the leader likes the person. Ethan says that if two people are equally qualified, a leader will spend more time with the one they enjoy, and that does not require kissing up but does reward being pleasant and helpful. He recalls hearing from Amazon leadership, he thinks Bezos, a test: when you enter a room, do you suck the oxygen out, or do people want you there? His rubric is whether people want you in the room.
Ethan acknowledges that engineers may dislike this and says he is trying to help, not to be liked. He is not apologizing for how the world works, and he wants people to know it.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: How do you win champions for a senior promotion packet when you have no natural collaboration with the leaders you need?
answer: Ethan's favorite method requires the manager to be on your side. As a manager, he would email peers or skip-level leaders to say that Ryan would be up for promotion in six months, that their group was adjacent, and that he would ask them for feedback. That gives them six months to watch, it does not feel self-serving since it focuses on their time, and six months later the leader cannot say they hardly saw the person. Ethan says he got good at getting people promoted, which helped him attract and keep talent; one person who missed a cycle gave him another six months, and the promotion came through.

If the manager is not on board, the next best option is for the person to approach the leaders and ask how to be in a natural position to give feedback over six months. Ethan advises oversubscribing, because of departures, reorgs and refusals: if you need four champions, ask six or seven. The ask can be framed as doing it properly and in advance, rather than as the usual last-minute request.

followups.question: A busy vice president may see such a request as low priority. How do you raise it?
answer: Ethan agrees it is low on their list, but says vice presidents also need other VPs to support their own promotions, so they know it is part of the system. To raise priority, find some relevance for them, answering what is in it for them, perhaps by showing how your work makes their life easier or faster. He says the system works largely because VPs understand it is the grease that keeps things flowing and can write approving feedback quickly.

For a manager who is supportive but passive, Ethan suggests coaching the manager, since the employee usually cares more about the career than the manager does. A middle ground is to ask the manager to send a short introduction asking the VP for a 15-minute meeting.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

followups.question: Can an engineer be promoted over the manager's objection?
answer: Ethan says he has never seen anyone promoted over their manager's objection. A big boss who overrules a manager creates a mess, because the manager would then have to work with a more senior person they did not support. Engineers who imagine being recognized despite a poor manager, he says, will not be. They must win the manager over or move to a manager who is on board.

He describes making a profession of getting people promoted quickly and fairly, and says it became his recruiting tool. His best employee started as a level-five engineer and went through senior engineer, manager, senior manager and director in eight years of working together, until he left to found a company. Ethan says they powered each other's careers and the example attracted others.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: What can someone who despises politics do to avoid it?
answer: Ethan gives two answers. First, choose a leader who shares the disdain, ideally from a similar technical background, and wants to reward the work. Second, work on the hardest area available, where expertise matters and the engineer stands out. He recalls Andy Jassy, then head of AWS, saying that a few principal engineers working on the hardest problems were relieved of the usual duties of reviewing architecture and mentoring because the company needed them solving those problems. Ethan notes that such engineers had the perfect boss.

He adds that a unique, valuable skill brings exceptions. When others complained that a high-level employee was not working at an Amazon level, Jassy said he agreed but that the person was in a role the company needed and knew it, so they would live with it. Ethan concludes that avoiding politics requires an essential skill and real leverage, which is the point of Cal Newport's So Good They Can't Ignore You.

followups.question: Does a growing company have less politics?
answer: Ethan believes so, and uses the post office as the extreme: roles are carrying mail or being postmaster, and there is only one postmaster until that person leaves. In a growing company, it is not twenty-five people wanting one promotion but many open opportunities. Over his 15 years at Amazon, he says, headcount grew from 14,000 to 1.4 million, a hundredfold. His first team had six people, and nine years later he led 800. He says that kind of growth opens doors that 5 or 10 percent annual growth does not, and his advice is to find high growth.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans

blocks.question: What advice would Ethan give his younger self about navigating corporate politics?
answer: Ethan wishes he could tell his early self that being right and technically astute is not enough, and that there is a lot more going on. He says he was blind to it or deprioritized it as management stuff, but management stuff controls the world even for an individual contributor. In a single sentence, he says people should take seriously that relationships are what actually control their progress.
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
